articles.title: Tidal Bans AI-Generated Music
articles.text:
The music streaming service Tidal said Tuesday that it would ban tracks it believes are completely AI-generated starting next month, a move its leader believes “will resonate with both artists and listeners alike.”

The service will remove the AI tracks starting Dec. 9, making Tidal the first music streaming platform to ban AI music entirely. It comes nearly five months after Tidal said it would demonetize any AI-powered song, force those artists to label their tracks as either AI-generated or AI-assisted and ban AI songs that were associated with “fraudulent activity,” a category that includes songs impersonating established artists and efforts to “deceive listeners.”

“But that’s enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done,” wrote Robert Andersen, the Tidal Lead at parent company Block, in an X thread on Tuesday. “We’ll begin removing all wholly AI-generated tracks from our catalog, and you’ll see them completely gone by the beginning of the year.”

Andersen said that 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays. The move will cleave the platform of 29 million tracks, he added, and have it reject between 80,000 to 85,000 songs a day.

“We encourage our peers to follow suit,” he wrote.

The move comes as competitors such as Spotify and Apple Music continue to test approaches to combat the rise of AI-generated tracks proliferating on their platforms, many of which the services have labeled some version of “slop” or “spam.” Apple Music said it would also begin labeling AI-generated or AI-assisted tracks on its platform, while Spotify said it would label artists it deemed AI creations as an “AI Persona.”

Spotify said in a blog post last month it also removed 50 million slop or spam tracks from users’ recommendations this year, which came after it removed 75 million of those songs from its catalog entirely. The revelation came among a number of updates regarding Spotify’s efforts to combat AI spam.

“This work isn’t finished,” Spotify added. “AI moves fast, and bad actors adapt just as fast. But as AI makes music more abundant, we believe listeners will value human artistry even more. Our job is to make Spotify the place they find it.”

articles.sourceTitle: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
articles.title: Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups
articles.text:
Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.

Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.

The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.

The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.

Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

articles.sourceTitle: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
articles.title: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
articles.text:
23rd November 2026 - Link Blog

GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer. GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights:

We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening.

I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.
It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.
I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.
Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.
It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.
I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

articles.title: Introducing Claude Ship | Claude by Anthropic
articles.text: Anyone who has opened a pull request knows how this goes. They start on the next thing, and then the review comes back. So they stop, dig back into the old code, push a fix, and wait for the review to run again. Then they go find someone to approve it.There's a good reason it works this way. Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that's easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now. On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.That's why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta. It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what's ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Claude Ship credits to use within 30 days of claiming. Claim by January 15, 2027. Terms apply.How Claude Ship works: review, fix, and approveClaude Ship is made up of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don't have to manage each step manually.Code Review performs an in-depth review of pull requests against the codebase through multiple lenses. It collects findings, adversarially verifies them, categorizes them, and posts them to a PR. On the Claude Code team, where Claude's review is one layer of a broader process, merged PRs more than doubled from June to September while the share reverted fell by more than 40%. Code Review gives teams fast reviews, clear findings, and a choice of Quick, Standard, or Deep review levels for each repository.PR Steward works to keep a PR green, but is designed not to approve or merge pull requests. It jumps in on failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback from Code Review, other review tools, or team members. After every push, it comments with what it changed and how to undo it. Developers can comment @claude with an instruction to steer the work, or @claude stop to have it step back.From there, Claude Approvals applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. Claude can approve routine changes on its own if the policy allows it, or can require deeper human sign-off for certain scenarios. It works like a smarter CODEOWNERS file. Teams can have Claude Approvals consider a variety of signals in its decision-making process, including Code Review findings or their own classifiers using natural language. For most customers, we recommend enabling this first in observe-only mode to build confidence before configuring branch protection to require Claude Approvals' green light.Two ways to get startedFor developers: /ship it from Claude CodeDevelopers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code. When a change is ready, they run /ship. Claude pushes it, opens the PR, reviews the change, and works on feedback and failing checks to help get it ready to merge. What can merge depends on the developer's permissions and the repository's branch rules.For admins and engineering leaders: set the rules, one repository at a timeTurning Claude Ship on for an entire repository puts it to work across a team's pull requests automatically, under settings and an approval policy the team controls. Developers don't need to manually invoke the /ship command.Admins choose where it runs. An admin turns on Code Review and PR Steward for each repository. Claude Approvals starts when a connected repository has a policy file on its default branch, and an admin can turn it off.Each repository gets the settings it needs. Admins choose the review level (Quick, Standard, or Deep), choose when reviews run, and configure spend limits.Teams keep the tools they have. Claude Ship works with existing branch protection and required checks.Teams set the pace. They can start with one repository, choose a review level and when reviews run, set a monthly spend limit, and run their approval policy in observe mode until they trust it.How the Claude Code team shipsWe run Claude Ship on many of our own pull requests. One of the biggest changes is who can act on customer feedback. For example, a product manager on the Claude Code team can now read a piece of feedback, talk through ideas and tradeoffs with Claude Tag, have it open a PR, and move on to the next thing while Claude Ship takes it through review, fixes, and an approval decision.Recently, a customer was confused because our Analytics API documentation implied an Admin key could pull Pro and Team usage. The PM asked Claude Tag whether a fix was in flight, and it opened one. Code Review found nothing blocking, a docs reviewer signed off, Claude Approvals passed, and the fix merged that same evening.What customers are sayingAvailabilityClaude Ship is available on Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, and PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.Claude Ship usage is billed on tokens, so turning it on can add to an organization’s costs. The amount depends on the number and size of pull requests covered, the review level, how often reviews run, and how much work PR Steward does. Admins can set spend limits for Code Review and PR Steward. Claude Approvals has no base charge, but classifiers in a policy are billed on the tokens they use, and a policy that uses Claude's review triggers a billed Code Review, even in observe mode. Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage.Claude Ship is not available to organizations with Zero Data Retention, the HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.Get startedDevelopers can update Claude Code and run /ship on their next change. /ship is rolling out in Claude Code and the desktop app starting today.Teams already using Code Review can add PR Steward on a repository, and an approval policy in observe mode.Teams new to Code Review can read the setup guide to connect GitHub and turn on their first repository.Learn more in documentation.

articles.sourceTitle: OpenAI reveals they solved VP ≠ VNP before Anthropic
articles.title: math/preprints/VP-and-VNP-are-different-November-23-2026 at main · openai/math · GitHub
articles.text:
OpenAI · November 23, 2026 edition
Theorem 1.1 gives a border arithmetic circuit size lower bound of
$\exp(\Omega((\log n)^{5/4}))$ for an explicit VNP family over every field.
Corollary 1.2 transfers the bound to the directed Hamiltonian cycle polynomial
over every field and to the permanent outside characteristic two.
The Lean proof of the exact VP–VNP separation
is also available in this repository.

The LaTeX source contains the full proof, with
TikZ figures and an editable bibliography.
To regenerate the PDF with Tectonic, run these commands from this directory.
cd build
tectonic Paper.tex
cp Paper.pdf ../paper.pdf
